newsitem.title: USA: Clinton names Albright as secretary of state. [CORRECTED 01:45 GMT 06/12]
newsitem.headline: Clinton names Albright as secretary of state. [CORRECTED 01:45 GMT 06/12]

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday nominated tough-talking U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright as the first woman secretary of state in U.S. history to lead a new national security team that will include a Republican as defence secretary.

In an Oval Office ceremony crowded with the nominees, their love ones and even one loser in the Cabinet sweepstakes, Clinton reached across party lines to select retiring Senator William Cohen of Maine for the defence post.
White House National Security Adviser Anthony Lake was chosen as the next director of the Central Intelligence Agency, and his NSA deputy, Samuel Berger, will succeed Lake.

All but Berger require Senate confirmation and the immediate reaction from the Republican-controlled Congress was favourable. "I believe it is a certainty that all four nominees ... will be viewed favourably by most senators," said Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a conservative Republican and frequent Clinton critic.

The Czech-born Albright, 59, elbowed her way into traditional male territory with praise from Clinton for a "steely determination" dating back to her youth when she was "raised in the shadow of Nazi aggression in Czechoslovakia."

Clinton denied he was appointing a woman to placate feminist groups who insisted he name women to senior jobs. Women voters backed him overwhelmingly in his re-election victory over Republican Bob Dole one month ago.

"It had nothing to do with her getting the job one way or the other," he told reporters. He said of all the candidates, "she had the best combination of qualities to succeed and to serve our country at this moment in history."
Even so, Clinton said with a grin, "My momma's smiling down at me right now." His strong-willed mother, Virginia Kelley, died of breast cancer in 1994 (corrects fom 1995).

Albright would be the highest-ranking woman ever in U.S. government. The secretary of state is fourth in line of succession to the presidency should Clinton be disabled, after the vice president, the speaker of the House of Representatives and the president pro tempore of the Senate.

The history of the moment was not lost on Albright, known for tough, plain talk in the erudite diplomatic atmosphere at the United Nations. Nodding to the man she is replacing, Warren Christopher, Albright said: "I can only hope that my heels can fill your shoes."

In Clinton's extended deliberations to fill an unusually large number of Cabinet openings, Albright won out over former Maine Senator George Mitchell, Clinton's envoy to Northern Ireland peace talks, and the president's former special envoy on Bosnia, Richard Holbrooke.

Addressing America's allies and rivals, Albright said: "We live in an era without power blocs in which old assumptions must be re-examined, institutions modernised and relationships transformed. If we are to master events rather than be mastered by them, we must be forward-looking in our thinking and flexible in our tactics."

Clinton also broke with tradition to pick Cohen to head the Defence Department and its huge annual budget. A moderate Republican, Cohen served 24 years in Congress -- 18 in the Senate -- and served on its Armed Services Committee.
He called Clinton's bipartisan move "a very bold and exciting move." It is unusual but not unprecedented for a president to make a Cabinet selection from the rival party.

"I particularly want to commend him for his willingness to reach across the aisle and send a very strong signal to the people of this country that he is dedicated to a bipartisan approach to the security of this country," Cohen said.

Clinton, asked if he was concerned about Cohen's reputation for an independent streak, said his administration "encourages people to be independent, to speak their mind, to argue for new ideas, to break new ground."
Standing out of camera range with a wan smile was CIA Director John Deutch, who lost out to Cohen among prospects to succeed Defence Secretary William Perry. Deutch is returning to private life.
Not present was Strobe Talbott, the Clinton friend who was reported to want Lake's job as national security adviser. Albright said he would stay on as deputy secretary of state.
Lake said as CIA director he wants to give Clinton "the unvarnished facts on which he conveys wise decisions in a time of change and promise."

Clinton aides said they hoped to have completed Cabinet selections by the end of the year and these would be announced piecemeal, in hopes the Senate would confirm at least some by the time Clinton's second-term inaugural on Jan. 20. They said more Republicans were under consideration.
